The conversion from glycolyl-CoA to glycolaldehyde requires 1 mol of NADH, while an additional 1 mol of NADH is necessary for the glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol conversion. Two mol of methanol generate 2 mol of formaldehyde, producing 2 mol of NADH. Subsequently, 1 mol of formaldehyde generates 1 mol of formyl-CoA, also yielding 1 mol of NADH, resulting in a total of 3 mol of NADH generated but only consuming 2 mol of NADH. When methanol is the sole carbon source (highlighted in yellow), the theoretical yield (mol/mol) is 50%, equivalent to a 0.97 theoretical yield (g/g). These calculations underscore the efficiency of our engineered pathways in utilizing different C1 compounds for ethylene glycol production, providing insights into their metabolic capabilities and potential for sustainable chemical manufacturing. In our lab’s initial HACL testing paper, we targeted formaldehyde (∆frmA) and formate (∆fdhF ∆fdnG ∆fdoG) oxidation, as well as glycolate utilization (∆glcD), to prevent competition or interference with the pathway’s performance and analysis (Chou et al., 2019). Subsequently, in our Nature Metabolism paper, we eliminated aldehyde dehydrogenases (aldh): ∆aldA, ∆aldB, ∆patD, ∆puuC, and endogenous thioesterases (ΔyciA, ΔtesA, ΔtesB, ΔybgC, ΔydiI, and ΔfadM) to further refine our study (Chou et al., 2021). In this research, we further knocked out the Acetate Kinase & Phosphate Acetyltransferase (ackA-pta) to enable the use of formate as an energy source in the pathway. Besides, since E. coli has a very strong ability to convert glycolaldehyde to glycolate, we knock out four main aldehyde dehydrogenases (aldA, aldB, pUUC, patD) to avoid the production of glycolate. 47 Develop a bioconversion process using genetically engineered microorganisms (Task 15) To determine the optimal time for ethylene glycol bioconversion, we conducted a time course experiment to monitor changes in the conversion profile (Figure 33). Given that glycolate and ethylene glycol differ only in the final enzymatic step, we replaced the enzyme responsible for converting glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol with Aldehyde dehydrogenase E. coli fucO. Formaldehyde is converted to formyl-CoA by Listeria monocytogenes (LmACR), and formyl-CoA and formaldehyde are condensed by Chloroflexi bacterium HGW-Chloroflexi-9 (CfhHACS).
